\title{Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety}
\shorttitle{Moment-to-Moment Affect}
\author{Micah G. Allen}
\affiliation{Center of Functionally Integrative Neuroscience, Department of Clinical Medicine, Aarhus University,
Aarhus, Denmark}
\authornote{Micah G. Allen, ORCID 0000-0001-9399-4179.

\textbf{Funding.} \funding

Corresponding author: Micah G. Allen, Center of Functionally Integrative Neuroscience, Aarhus University,
Aarhus, Denmark. E-mail: micah@cfin.au.dk.}

\abstract{Watching others in danger can evoke anxiety and bodily discomfort even when viewers remain physically
safe. We present an open-source browser-based platform for characterising how these experiences unfold over time. The
platform collects simultaneous ratings of valence and arousal within a video, synchronised to film time, and combines
them with participant training, automatic handling of viewing interruptions and checks of data integrity, enabling
online characterisation of stimuli before laboratory use. We demonstrate its application to a 13.5-min first-person
film of dangerous activities at height, presented without sound. Participants continuously rated their own affect and
completed a measure of somatic anxiety before and after viewing. An exploratory sample ($n$~=~\val{n_exploratory})
informed preregistered tests in an independent confirmatory sample ($N$~=~\val{n_primary}). Arousal rose, remained
elevated for several minutes and declined towards the end, while valence was more unpleasant during the sustained
phase than during the opening. The temporal shape of group-average responses closely reproduced across samples.
Somatic anxiety increased substantially after viewing ($d_z$~=~\val{H1:est}), with larger increases associated with
higher arousal and more unpleasant valence. The film provides a characterised induction of sustained unpleasant
arousal accompanied by changes in reported bodily experience. The openly available platform, data and reference
trajectories support its reuse and the characterisation of other stimuli for research linking subjective emotion to
physiological and neural responses.}

\keywords{emotion induction, film, continuous ratings, valence and arousal, somatic anxiety}

% Micah's revision (2026-10-10) restructured in revision three: the online measurement challenge and the platform
% now come before the film, which is introduced as the demonstration. No "Introduction" heading (journal rule; the
% heading added earlier on 2026-10-11 was removed again when the journal checklist was applied).

Watching someone hang from the edge of a skyscraper can be uncomfortable even from the safety of a chair. As the
danger unfolds, concern for the person on screen may be accompanied by tension and other bodily sensations. This
makes vicarious danger a useful setting in which to study how emotional experience develops over time. For research
linking emotion to behaviour, physiology or brain activity, the timing of that experience matters: a measure taken
after an episode cannot show when arousal built or how long it persisted \parencite{saarimaki2021naturalistic}.

Films allow researchers to present the same unfolding events to different viewers. Established film libraries have
demonstrated their value for eliciting emotion, commonly using ratings collected after viewing
\parencite{gilman2017film,gross1995emotion,schaefer2010assessing}. Continuous ratings extend this approach by tracing
experience within a film \parencite{ruef2007continuous}. In naturalistic neuroimaging, such ratings have been related
to neural responses and brain-state dynamics \parencite{chang2021endogenous,goldin2005neural}. Resources such as
Emo-FilM combine moment-to-moment emotion annotations with physiological and fMRI recordings
\parencite{morgenroth2025emofilm}, and continuous anxiety ratings have been used to follow the suspense of a Hitchcock
thriller \parencite{kirk2024brainheart}. These measurements also make it possible to ask whether different viewers
experience changes in emotion at similar points in the same film.

Collecting such ratings online makes large and diverse samples accessible, but it raises practical demands.
Interpreting a rating requires knowing when it was made relative to the images on screen, and whether the film played
and the participant took part as intended. Buffering, switching to another browser tab or a lapse in rating can break
the link between a response and the moment it describes, and remote participants are not observed. Unsupervised
online studies must also contend with AI-assisted and automated responding
\parencite{sehgal2026aiassisted,veselovsky2023artificial,westwood2025existential}.

We developed an open-source browser-based platform to meet these demands. Viewers report how they feel by moving a
point within an affect grid embedded in the video, rating valence and arousal simultaneously and in synchrony with
film time. This two-dimensional approach captures both how pleasant an experience feels and how activating it is
\parencite{russell1980circumplex,russell1989affectgrid}, building on established methods for continuous affect rating
\parencite{schubert1999measuring,girard2018darma}. Beyond the rating itself, the platform contributes three things. It
records each rating together with the video time and the time of the frame actually presented; it pauses the film
when viewing is interrupted and saves data periodically, so that sessions survive interruptions and page reloads; and
it trains participants before the film and records the input and text-entry events needed to assess the integrity of
each session (Online Resource 1, Fig.~S1). Continuous rating tools exist for desktop media annotation
\parencite{girard2014carma,girard2018darma} and immersive virtual reality \parencite{fourcade2025affecttracker}, and
browser-based tools already support continuous annotation of video, including in online studies
\parencite{boccignone2017amhuse,louven2022emotouch,melhart2019pagan,farrens2020continuous}. The contribution therefore lies not in
browser-based continuous rating itself but in combining frame-referenced timing, presentation control, training and
integrity checks in one open workflow.

We demonstrate the platform with a 13.5-min first-person film of people climbing and performing unsecured stunts on a
skyscraper. Presented without sound, the film centres on visually apparent danger that can be followed without
spoken dialogue (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}a). Its progression towards a prolonged period of danger makes it a
promising stimulus for studying sustained unpleasant arousal. An extended episode of this kind could help researchers
examine how emotional and bodily responses change as a threatening situation continues. To use it for this purpose,
however, we first need to establish whether viewers show a reproducible affective time course and report an
accompanying increase in bodily symptoms of anxiety. Before and after viewing, participants therefore also completed
the somatic subscale of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA), which assesses symptoms
such as a fast heartbeat and muscle tension \parencite{gros2007psychometric,ree2008distinguishing}. These measures
allow us to relate the unfolding affective response to changes in reported bodily experience, a central concern of
interoception research \parencite{cristaldi2026beyond,critchley2017interoception}.

An exploratory sample ($n$~=~\val{n_exploratory}) informed preregistered hypotheses tested in an independent
confirmatory sample ($N$~=~\val{n_primary}). We predicted that arousal would rise, remain elevated and then decline,
with more unpleasant valence during the sustained period than during the opening. We also predicted an increase in
somatic anxiety and replication of the group-level affective time course. Further hypotheses tested whether fear of
heights was associated with a stronger response, whether increases in somatic anxiety accompanied higher arousal and
more unpleasant valence, and whether retrospective anxiety ratings converged with plateau arousal and somatic change.
The study therefore evaluates both the film as a sustained anxiety induction and the platform as a means of
characterising affective dynamics online.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Preregistration and Transparency}

The hypotheses and analysis plan were preregistered on OSF (\url{https://osf.io/s2yvb}). All confirmatory tests
followed the registered analysis plan; exploratory analyses are identified as such.

\subsection{Rating Platform and Data Integrity}

The rating platform we developed for this study (open source, MIT licence) is a jsPsych task
\parencite{deleeuw2023jspsych} hosted on a JATOS server \parencite{lange2015jatos} that runs in an ordinary desktop web
browser; the version used here is archived as \texttt{v1.0-heights-film} (see Data Availability). Its key features
are as follows. Ratings are given on a small affect grid \parencite{russell1989affectgrid} overlaid on the video
(Figure~\ref{fig:overview}a; Online Resource 1, Fig.~S2): the mouse pointer is hidden and locked, so moving the mouse moves the dot without
clicking, with horizontal position coding valence (0~=~unpleasant, 100~=~pleasant) and vertical position arousal
(0~=~low, 100~=~high). The position is sampled at 20~Hz with video, frame and elapsed time, and every raw input event
is stored. The film is downloaded in full before playback, controls and seeking are disabled, leaving the tab or full
screen pauses the film, and data are saved every 30~s so that a session resumes after a page reload. Before the film,
participants practise with the same mouse control by tracking a moving target and by placing six everyday situations
on the grid, with feedback. The same session presents standard self-report formats (Likert-type scales,
multiple-choice and checklist items, and free-text entry). Data integrity is supported by two instructed-response
attention checks, blocked pasting and logged keystrokes in text fields, counts of script-generated browser events,
and quality-control code that summarises coverage, interruptions and rating activity and flags unusual mouse movement
and text entry for review. Participants were excluded solely by the registered rules (Online Resource 1, Table~S1).
Section S1 of Online Resource 1 describes each feature in detail, and its Fig.~S1 shows the session workflow.

\subsection{Participants}

Participants were recruited on Prolific \parencite{palan2018prolific}, with filters for fluent English, normal or
corrected-to-normal vision, an approval rate of at least 95\%, at least 20 previous submissions and a desktop
computer with a mouse or trackpad. They
were recruited in cohorts with a 50/50 quota on Prolific's sex screener and were paid \pounds 4.80. The information
sheet advised people with a strong fear of heights not to take part. The pilot and the first cohort formed the
exploratory sample, which was used to fix the segment edges, exclusion rules and sample size; later cohorts formed the
confirmatory sample, on which all confirmatory tests were run. Recruitment stopped at the end of the first cohort after
which at least 120 usable confirmatory participants were available, a number giving 80\% power to detect correlations
of about .25. The study involved watching a film and answering questionnaires and was not a health research project
under the Danish Act on Research Ethics Review of Health Research Projects and Health Data Research Projects; for such
studies there is no legal requirement for ethical approval in Denmark, and Aarhus University does not require it. The
Aarhus University Research Ethics Committee provides a standard statement to this effect. All participants gave informed consent online before taking part.

\subsection{Stimulus}

The stimulus was a 13 min 28 s first-person video of an unsecured climb to the roof of a skyscraper
\parencite{tikhomirov2017dubai}, presented without sound (1,280~$\times$~720 pixels, 25 frames per second) and
downloaded in full before playback.

\subsection{Procedure and Measures}

After consent and a device check, participants rated their everyday fear of heights (\enquote{In everyday life, how
afraid are you of heights?}, 1--7) and completed the practice. They then completed the somatic subscale of the STICSA
(11 items, 1--4, total 11--44, state instructions; \cite{ree2008distinguishing}), watched the film while rating
continuously, and completed the STICSA again immediately afterwards. Instructions asked participants how they felt at
that moment. Afterwards, participants rated how tense or anxious they had felt overall while watching (1--7) and
answered further questions on their experience and data quality. Participants also provided a written account of what
they saw and how the film made them feel (minimum 100 words), with a separate optional field for feedback on the study
or technical difficulties.

\subsection{Data Processing and Exclusions}

Ratings were resampled to 1~Hz of film time (808 values) by linear interpolation. The film was divided into four
preregistered segments, estimated in the exploratory sample by piecewise-linear segmentation of group-mean arousal:
baseline (0--262~s), rise (262--470~s), plateau (470--692~s) and return (692--808~s). Participants were excluded if
they failed both attention checks, produced script-generated input, did not type their written description (fewer
than 0.2 keystrokes per character for descriptions of at least 200 characters), gave erratic input (more than 10\%
of mouse movements larger than 250 pixels), had
disrupted viewing (more than 30~s of buffering or 60~s of interruptions), had ratings during fewer than 95\% of the
film, or had seen the film before (Online Resource 1, Table~S1).

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}

All tests were two-sided ($\alpha$~=~.05) with Holm correction within each hypothesis family; directional hypotheses
counted as supported only if significant in the predicted direction. H1 compared STICSA totals after and before the
film (paired $t$ test; $d_z$ with exact 95\% CI; Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a check). H2 tested four contrasts
between participants' segment means (arousal: rise $>$ baseline, plateau $>$ baseline, return $<$ plateau; valence:
plateau $<$ baseline) with paired $t$ tests. H3 correlated the confirmatory and exploratory group-mean series (Pearson
$r$; 95\% CI from 5,000 circular block bootstrap resamples with 30-s blocks) and was supported if the lower bound exceeded .50.
H4--H6 were Spearman correlations with bootstrap 95\% CIs (5,000 resamples): everyday fear of heights with plateau
arousal, plateau valence and STICSA change (H4); STICSA change with whole-film arousal and valence (H5); and post-film
anxiety with STICSA change and plateau arousal (H6). Two registered sensitivity samples (stricter engagement criteria;
participants rejected on Prolific removed) repeated all tests. Exploratory analyses examined the change in each STICSA
item (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected across items) and the effects of age and sex (mixed models of segment
means). Analyses were run in Python \val{python_version} with NumPy,
SciPy, pandas and statsmodels. Large language model tools (ChatGPT and Codex, OpenAI; Claude Code, Anthropic) assisted
with writing and testing the analysis code and with preparing the manuscript. The analysis code was checked with tests
on small simulated datasets with known answers, and the author verified the analyses, results and references and takes
full responsibility for the work.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Online Implementation and Data Quality}

Of \val{pq:conf:completed} completed
confirmatory sessions, \val{pq:conf:usable} (\val{pq:conf:pct_usable}\% of completed sessions) met the registered
criteria: \val{n_excl_disrupted} were excluded for disrupted viewing, \val{n_excl_freetext} for an untyped written
account and \val{n_excl_erratic} for erratic input (exploratory sample: \val{pq:expl:usable} of
\val{pq:expl:completed} completed sessions). No session was excluded for script-generated input, low coverage, failing
both attention checks or having seen the film. Ratings covered a median of \val{pq:conf:coverage_median}\% of film
seconds (minimum \val{pq:conf:coverage_min}\%). Buffering occurred in \val{pq:conf:n_any_buffering} sessions and
interruptions in \val{pq:conf:n_any_interruption} (longest \val{pq:conf:buffering_max}~s and
\val{pq:conf:interrupted_max}~s). \val{pq:conf:att_none} participants passed both attention checks and
\val{pq:conf:att_one} failed one; \val{pq:conf:attentive_yes} reported watching with full attention,
\val{pq:conf:attentive_mostly} mostly and \val{pq:conf:attentive_no} not.
Among retained participants, ratings changed in a median of \val{pq:conf:bouts_median} bouts per minute
(interquartile range \val{pq:conf:bouts_q1}--\val{pq:conf:bouts_q3}), and the median longest stretch without input
was \val{pq:conf:gap_median}~s, which may reflect holding the dot still while feelings were unchanged;
\val{pq:conf:n_sparse} met the registered definition of sparse rating and were removed in the stricter sensitivity
sample. Split-half reliability of the group-mean series was \val{rel:arousal} for arousal and \val{rel:valence} for
valence. Page reloads were not part of the exported data. The retained sample had a mean age of \val{age_mean} years ($SD$~=~\val{age_sd}; \val{n_female}
female, \val{n_male} male, \val{n_sex_missing} not available). Sample characteristics, descriptive statistics and all
confirmatory tests, including both sensitivity samples, are given in Online Resource 1 (Tables S2--S5).

\subsection{Somatic Anxiety and Affective Time Course}

\paragraph{Somatic anxiety (H1).} STICSA somatic scores rose by \val{H1:diff} points from before
($M$~=~\val{sticsa_pre_mean}, $SD$~=~\val{sticsa_pre_sd}) to after the film ($M$~=~\val{sticsa_post_mean},
$SD$~=~\val{sticsa_post_sd}), \val{H1:report} (Figure~\ref{fig:sticsa}a). Scores rose for \val{n_increase}
participants and fell for \val{n_decrease}, and the Wilcoxon test agreed (\val{H1:wilcoxon}). In an exploratory item
analysis, all eleven items increased ($p_\mathrm{Holm}$ \val{items:pholm_max}; Figure~\ref{fig:sticsa}b and
Online Resource 1, Table~S6), most of all a fast heartbeat ($d_z$~=~\val{items:rank1:dz}) and least a dry throat, weak
muscles and stiff limbs ($d_z$~=~\val{items:rank11:dz}--\val{items:rank9:dz}).

\paragraph{Time course (H2, H3).} Arousal was higher in the rise segment than at baseline, \val{H2a:report}, and in the plateau than at baseline,
\val{H2b:report}. It was lower in the
final segment than on the plateau, \val{H2c:report} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}b; Online Resource 1, Fig.~S3). Valence was lower on the plateau
than at baseline, \val{H2d:report} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}c). The group-mean series of the
confirmatory sample closely followed the shape of the exploratory sample's series, for arousal, \val{H3arousal:report},
and for valence, \val{H3valence:report}.

\paragraph{Individual differences (H4--H6).} Participants whose STICSA scores rose more gave higher whole-film arousal
ratings, \val{H5a:report}, and lower valence ratings, \val{H5b:report} (Figure~\ref{fig:sticsa}c, d). Post-film anxiety correlated with STICSA
change, \val{H6a:report}, and with plateau arousal, \val{H6b:report}. Everyday fear of heights was associated with
more negative plateau valence, \val{H4b:report}; its associations with plateau arousal, \val{H4a:report}, and with
STICSA change, \val{H4c:report}, were not significant after correction (Online Resource 1, Fig.~S4, shows all individual-difference tests).

\paragraph{Somatic anxiety and ratings by segment (exploratory).} In a post hoc exploratory analysis of both samples
($n$~=~\val{xseg:n}), STICSA change was correlated with the mean ratings in each segment (Spearman $\rho$ with
bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals, uncorrected; Figure~\ref{fig:sticsasegments}). There was no clear
association at baseline (arousal \val{xseg:arousal:baseline}; valence \val{xseg:valence:baseline}).
Valence was associated with STICSA change in the rise (\val{xseg:valence:rise}) and plateau
(\val{xseg:valence:plateau}), and arousal in the plateau (\val{xseg:arousal:plateau}) but less clearly in the rise
(\val{xseg:arousal:rise}). Associations were weaker in the return (arousal \val{xseg:arousal:return}; valence
\val{xseg:valence:return}).

\paragraph{Sensitivity and additional analyses.} All registered support decisions were unchanged in both sensitivity samples
($n$~=~\val{n_stricter} and \val{n_without_rejected}; Online Resource 1, Table~S5). In a registered descriptive analysis,
re-estimating the segment edges in the
confirmatory sample placed them at \val{edge1:est}, \val{edge2:est} and \val{edge3:est}~s, against the registered
\val{edge1:reg}, \val{edge2:reg} and \val{edge3:reg}~s. Exploratory analyses described where on the affect grid ratings fell in each segment (Online Resource 1, Fig.~S5)
and found no evidence that the time course differed by sex
(arousal: \val{agesex:arousal:sex_x_segment}; valence: \val{agesex:valence:sex_x_segment}) or by age, or that
STICSA change was associated with sex or age (Online Resource 1, Table~S7 and Figs.~S6--S7).

\section{Discussion}
% Micah's revision (2026-10-10), reordered in revision three: platform second, then safeguards; reuse paragraph added.

A film of other people in danger produced a sustained, reproducible affective response in viewers who remained
physically safe. Arousal increased and stayed elevated for several minutes before declining, while the sustained
period was experienced as more unpleasant than the opening. The temporal shape closely reproduced across independent
samples, and somatic anxiety increased substantially after viewing ($d_z$~=~\val{H1:est}). Participants reporting
larger increases in bodily symptoms also rated the film as more arousing and unpleasant. Exploratory analyses
suggest that this link is phase-specific: it was absent at baseline and strongest during the rise and
plateau, which argues against a general rating tendency and ties the bodily response to the film's danger phases.
Together, these findings
establish a characterised episode of vicarious danger in which affective dynamics can be studied alongside changes in
felt bodily state.

The platform makes stimulus exposure, response timing and the quality of participation inspectable within
one workflow. Each rating is stored with the video time and the time of the presented frame, interruptions pause the
film and are logged, and the same logs feed the registered exclusion rules and sensitivity analyses. In the
confirmatory sample, \val{pq:conf:pct_usable}\% of completed sessions met the registered criteria, and ratings
covered a median of \val{pq:conf:coverage_median}\% of the film. The platform also makes this approach available for other stimuli and research settings. It collects simultaneous valence
and arousal ratings within the video in an ordinary browser, allowing films to be characterised online before
laboratory use. It complements established desktop annotation software \parencite{girard2014carma,girard2018darma}
and tools for immersive virtual reality \parencite{fourcade2025affecttracker}, as well as other browser-based
annotation tools. Applied across films, the same
procedure could identify stimuli with different durations or patterns of unpleasant arousal and test how consistently
these patterns reproduce. The combination of a characterised stimulus, reference trajectories and reusable software
gives other researchers a practical starting point for such comparisons.

Making participation inspectable matters because unsupervised online studies face AI-assisted and automated
responding. Estimates of its prevalence vary widely across platforms, tasks and methods, from about 1\% of submissions
among Prolific workers who shared their ChatGPT histories \parencite{sehgal2026aiassisted} to 33--46\% of crowd
workers on a text summarisation task on Amazon Mechanical Turk \parencite{veselovsky2023artificial}. Where assistance
occurs, it is rarely caught: on Prolific, assisted submissions were approved for payment 99.6\% of the time, and half
involved bounded responses such as choices and ratings rather than free text \parencite{sehgal2026aiassisted}. Fully
automated agents can also pass standard attention checks while simulating human reading times, mouse movements and
keystrokes \parencite{westwood2025existential}. The platform therefore applies safeguards to both the continuous
ratings and the written reports: copying and pasting are blocked, input events and text entry are logged, synthetic
input, implausible mouse movement and duplicated or LLM-typical text are flagged, and viewing interruptions are
recorded. Continuous ratings
that must follow the film second by second are also harder to delegate than a single
questionnaire answer. These features add friction against some forms of assisted or automated responding and support
transparent review of questionable sessions, but agents that simulate human input could evade them, and the present
study does not estimate their detection accuracy.

The reproducibility of the time course is particularly useful for research on sustained emotion. Correlations between
the exploratory and confirmatory group trajectories were \val{H3arousal:est} for arousal and \val{H3valence:est} for
valence, providing a common temporal reference for subsequent studies using the same stimulus. Researchers can use
this reference to select intervals in which arousal is rising or remains elevated, and to examine responses as it
declines. It could also inform affective regressors in independent neuroimaging samples, alongside relevant visual and
event-related features \parencite{goldin2005neural,saarimaki2021naturalistic}. These correlations establish similarity
in group-level temporal shape; they do not establish absolute agreement or reliability within individual viewers.
Indeed, the confirmatory sample reported somewhat higher arousal during the opening and final minutes. The reference
trajectory should therefore guide the study of individual experience without being assumed to describe every
participant.

The accompanying increase in somatic anxiety connects these shared dynamics to how viewers experienced their bodies.
In the exploratory item analysis, all eleven symptoms increased, with the largest change in reports of a fast
heartbeat. Larger increases in somatic anxiety were associated with higher average arousal and more unpleasant
valence, while retrospective anxiety ratings converged with both somatic change and plateau arousal. Everyday fear of
heights was associated with more unpleasant plateau valence, although its associations with arousal and somatic change
were not significant after correction. Anticipation, concern for the climbers and discomfort at the views of height
may all contribute to the experience.

These findings offer a basis for examining how bodily responses and their perception contribute to sustained emotion.
Interoception research requires ways to study bodily experience during ongoing emotional experiences
\parencite{cristaldi2026beyond,critchley2017interoception}. The present film provides an extended period of unpleasant
arousal together with an increase in reported bodily symptoms. A next step is to record cardiac, respiratory and
electrodermal activity during viewing \parencite{kreibig2010autonomic}, allowing researchers to test whether
physiological responses follow the shared affective course and whether their relationship to subjective experience
changes over the film. Combined with fMRI, these measures could help explain how neural representations of bodily
signals relate to felt emotion during a sustained episode. The current data establish the subjective response; they
leave its physiological basis and temporal relationship to bodily change open.

Other laboratories can reuse the task, the quality-control code and the deployment scripts, and the exact
version used here is preserved (\texttt{v1.0-heights-film}). In the current release (\texttt{v1.1.0}), a new study is set up by
replacing the video and editing a single study file, which holds the participant-facing texts, questionnaires,
recruitment settings and quality-control thresholds, and a tutorial describes the steps.

The findings also define the scope of this approach. Without a control film, we cannot isolate the contribution
of heights or establish specificity relative to other intense films. Continuous rating may influence the experience,
so the trajectories should be evaluated before they are transferred to passive viewing
\parencite{hutcherson2005attention}. Somatic symptoms were assessed only before and after the film, leaving their time
course unresolved, and \val{pct_floor_pre}\% of participants began at the scale minimum and could not report a
decrease. The final reduction in arousal does not establish a return to a pre-film baseline. The platform's integrity checks were not validated against known assisted or automated sessions, and the frame timestamp depends on browser support. Online recruitment and
the advice that people with a strong fear of heights should not participate also limit generalisation, particularly
to people with severe height-related fear.

The film and platform provide a reusable way to study an emotional episode with a reproducible group-level time
course and a substantial change in reported somatic anxiety. This common reference makes it possible to ask how
people differ in their responses to the same unfolding danger, and how those differences relate to the physiology and
neural processes underlying emotional experience.

(\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23151387}). The film is a third-party video
that is publicly available on YouTube \parencite{tikhomirov2017dubai} and is not redistributed.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\caption{The Rating Screen and Continuous Arousal and Valence Ratings Over the Film}
\label{fig:overview}
\label{fig:timecourse}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.53\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Fig1.pdf}
\figurenote{(a) The rating screen at 10:36, during the scene in which a member of the group is held by one hand over
the edge (composite illustration: film frame from \textcite{tikhomirov2017dubai} with the rating grid redrawn as it
appears in the task). Participants moved the dot within the affect grid with the mouse: left to right for unpleasant
to pleasant, down to up for low to high activation (arousal). The dot marks the confirmatory sample's mean rating at
that moment (valence \val{task:valence}, arousal \val{task:arousal}). (b) Arousal (0~=~low, 100~=~high) and (c)
valence (0~=~unpleasant, 50~=~neutral, 100~=~pleasant), rated continuously and resampled to 1~Hz. Thin lines are
individual participants of the confirmatory sample; the thick line is the group mean with its 95\% confidence
interval ($N$~=~\val{n_primary}); the dashed line is the group mean of the exploratory sample
($n$~=~\val{n_exploratory}). Shading marks the four preregistered segments, estimated from group-mean arousal in the
exploratory sample; the dotted line marks 10:36.}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\caption{Somatic Anxiety Before and After the Film and Its Relation to the Ratings}
\label{fig:sticsa}
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{Fig2.pdf}
\figurenote{(a) STICSA somatic totals (11--44) before and after the film in the confirmatory sample
($N$~=~\val{n_primary}). Grey lines connect each participant's scores; boxes show medians and interquartile ranges;
the black line shows means with 95\% confidence intervals; H1: \val{H1:report}. (b) Share of participants giving each answer (1~=~not at all
to 4~=~very much so) to the eleven somatic items before (top) and after (bottom) the film; items are ordered as in the
questionnaire, and the two highest answers are hatched. (c, d) STICSA change (after minus before) against each participant's whole-film mean arousal
and valence (registered H5a and H5b). Points are participants (jittered sideways); the black line is a least-squares
fit and the grey band its 95\% confidence interval, shown as a visual guide. Spearman correlations with bootstrap
95\% confidence intervals: (c) H5a, \val{H5a:report}; (d) H5b, \val{H5b:report}.}
